principles: Records kept for a purpose not yet stated
An easy way that goes unused

world_behind.title: This is a transfer of custody
world_behind.text: Verse 1 commands Helaman to take the records. Mosiah 28 records the same handover to Alma, and Alma 63 will record Helaman passing them to Shiblon.

world_behind.title: Three sets of objects change hands
world_behind.text: The plates of Nephi, the plates of brass, and the twenty-four Jaredite plates with the interpreters. Alma treats each separately and gives a reason for each.

world_behind.title: Alma does not know the whole purpose
world_behind.text: Verse 11 says the mysteries are not yet fully made known to him and he will forbear. He hands over objects whose full use he cannot explain.

world_behind.title: He can name one purpose already fulfilled
world_behind.text: Verse 9 says Ammon and his brethren could not have convinced the Lamanites without the records. Alma 17 through 26 is the evidence he is citing.

world_behind.title: Gazelem is named once in scripture
world_behind.text: Verse 23 quotes the Lord promising a servant by that name a stone that shines in darkness. Alma gives the quotation and does not identify the servant.

world_behind.title: Liahona is a Lamanite-era word the record translates
world_behind.text: Verse 38 supplies the gloss: a compass. Alma 18 did the same for Rabbanah, and both glosses appear where a term carries something English will not.

world_behind.title: The Liahona lesson is about neglect
world_behind.text: Verses 40 through 42 say it worked by faith, that the fathers were slothful, and that they wandered and went hungry. Alma applies the same to the word of Christ.

words.text: To shake through a sieve, separating what falls from what stays. The record uses it twice and the King James Bible three times, including Christ telling Simon that Satan has desired to sift him as wheat. Alma uses chaff instead of wheat, which leaves nothing behind.

The instrument for translating a record. It appears six times in the record, and never in the King James Bible. Mosiah 8 and 28 explain what they do; Alma hands them over with the twenty-four plates they are for.
A name, given once in scripture, inside a quotation from the Lord about a servant and a stone that shines in darkness. Alma quotes it without explanation, and the record never says who is meant.

The ball or director prepared for Lehi's family, glossed here as a compass. The word occurs once in scripture. Alma supplies both the term the fathers used and the translation, and then spends nine verses on what it was for.

A valley. The King James Bible uses the word nine times and always of actual ground; the record uses it once, and Alma makes it a figure for this life. His phrase is a vale of sorrow set against a better land of promise.

Serious, self-controlled, unintoxicated. The record uses it four times and the King James Bible twelve, usually as an instruction to church officers. Alma's last word to Helaman before farewell is to be sober.

phrases.term: For it is for a wise purpose that they are kept
phrases.text: Alma gives a reason that withholds itself. He repeats the phrase in verses 12, 14, and 18, and each time the purpose stays with God. The records are handed over on trust.

phrases.term: If they are kept they must retain their brightness
phrases.text: A promise about physical objects, stated as a condition. Keeping them preserves them, and Alma extends the claim to all the plates containing holy writ.

phrases.term: By small and simple things are great things brought to pass
phrases.text: The chapter's most quoted line, and it appears here as a defense. Alma has just said his son may think this is foolishness, and this is his answer to that objection.

phrases.term: Ammon and his brethren could not have convinced so many thousands of the Lamanites
phrases.text: The one purpose Alma can point to as already accomplished. The mission of Alma 17 through 26 succeeded because there were records to teach from, and he names the result rather than the theory.

phrases.term: These mysteries are not yet fully made known unto me; therefore I shall forbear
phrases.text: Alma stops talking at the edge of what he knows. He says so plainly to his son, in the middle of handing over the objects the mysteries belong to.

phrases.term: His course is one eternal round
phrases.text: A phrase used three times in this record. Alma offers it as the reason a withheld purpose can be trusted: the counsel is wise, the paths are straight, and the pattern does not change.

phrases.term: O remember, remember, my son Helaman, how strict are the commandments of God
phrases.text: The doubled verb is the chapter's habit. Alma repeats remember at verses 13, 14, 32, 34, and 35, and the instruction is always attached to something specific rather than general.

phrases.term: He may sift you as chaff before the wind
phrases.text: The warning attached to transgression. Christ told Simon that Satan wanted to sift him as wheat, where something is left; Alma's version leaves nothing, since chaff is what the wind takes.

phrases.term: It did work for them according to their faith in God
phrases.text: The operating principle of the Liahona, stated once. The spindles pointed when the fathers believed they would, and verse 41 says the works ceased when the faith and diligence did.

phrases.term: It is as easy to give heed to the word of Christ
phrases.text: Alma's application, built on the comparison he has just made. The easiness is the point of the whole passage, and verse 46 turns it into the warning: do not be slothful because of the easiness of the way.
Five words, near the end of the charge. Alma has used the brass serpent in Alma 33 and returns to the same figure here, compressed into an instruction to his son.

verses.label: v. 1–2
verses.title: One verb, five times, in three different senses
verses.text: Verse 2 turns on keep: keep a record, keep these things sacred, keep them as I have kept them, kept for a wise purpose. What Helaman is handed is not a box but a practice, and the charge is stated as a continuation, not a handover. The record has Alma define the office by repeating its verb until it covers writing, preserving and revering alike.

verses.label: v. 7
verses.title: The claim is made and then made again
verses.text: Having said in verse 6 that great things come of small ones, Alma restates it whole in verse 7 instead of developing it: "the Lord God doth work by means to bring about his great and eternal purposes; and by very small means the Lord doth confound the wise." Repetition does the work an argument would, and the chapter will come back to the same idea at verse 41 to explain a compass.

verses.label: v. 27–29
verses.title: A record-keeper is given a redaction rule
verses.text: The oaths, covenants, agreements, signs and wonders are to be retained but withheld: "ye shall keep these secret plans of their oaths and their covenants from this people, and only their wickedness and their murders and their abominations shall ye make known unto them." Preserve everything, publish part. The reason given is contagion and not discretion: "lest peradventure they should fall into darkness also and be destroyed."

verses.label: v. 38
verses.title: One object, four names, and a gloss
verses.text: "The thing which our fathers call a ball, or director—or our fathers called it Liahona, which is, being interpreted, a compass." Two of the names are attributed to the fathers, one is offered as a translation, and the record supplies the last for readers who evidently needed it. A sentence about an instrument spends most of its length on what to call it.

chapter.title: Alma hands over what he cannot fully explain
chapter.text: He says four times that the purpose is wise and known to God, and once that he does not know the mysteries yet. The trust is in the keeping rather than in the understanding.

chapter.title: He argues for small means as a principle
chapter.text: Anticipating that his son will think this is foolishness, Alma states the rule and then demonstrates it twice: the records converting thousands, and the Liahona steering a family.

chapter.title: The one proven purpose is a mission the reader just watched
chapter.text: Ammon and his brethren could not have done it without the brass plates. Alma 17 through 26 becomes the evidence for Alma 37's argument.

chapter.title: Remember is the chapter's engine
chapter.text: It appears at verses 13, 14, 32, 34, and 35, doubled at least once, and it always attaches to a named thing rather than to a mood.

chapter.title: He tells his son what to withhold
chapter.text: The oaths and signs of the destroyed people are to be kept back while their wickedness is made known. Alma is teaching editorial judgment over a record.

chapter.title: The Liahona failed by neglect and not by breaking
chapter.text: It worked by faith, the faith lapsed, and the family wandered. Alma names slothfulness as the cause and applies it directly to scripture reading.

chapter.title: Easiness is treated as the danger
chapter.text: Verse 46 warns against letting an easy way make a man idle. The chapter's warning is about a remedy that costs nothing and therefore gets ignored, which is the brass serpent argument of Alma 33 again.

chapter.title: The charge ends in four short imperatives
chapter.text: Take care, look to God, declare the word, be sober. After forty-six verses of explanation, Alma closes with instructions a young man can carry.

applications.title: Keep the thing whose purpose you cannot yet state
applications.text: Alma hands over records "for a wise purpose" and concedes at verse 12 that "which purpose is known unto God." Custody does not require comprehension. Some of what you have been given to look after will not explain itself for years.

applications.title: Do the small thing on principle
applications.text: The rule is stated twice, "by small and simple things are great things brought to pass," and "by very small means the Lord doth confound the wise." Alma anticipates being thought foolish and says so before he is told. Pick the small thing you have been discounting and do it anyway.

applications.title: Say what the record has actually done
applications.text: He does not argue the plates matter in the abstract. He gives their effect: they "enlarged the memory of this people," convinced many of their errors, and brought them to the knowledge of God. When you defend keeping something, name the work it has done.

applications.title: Stop where your knowledge stops
applications.text: Alma refuses to speculate about the interpreters, "the mysteries of God are not fully made known unto me; therefore I shall forbear." The refusal costs him nothing and it is stated in the middle of a charge to his son.

applications.title: Guard the material that could be misused
applications.text: He tells Helaman to keep the oaths and covenants of the secret combinations back, "trust not those secret plans unto this people," and to teach an everlasting hatred of the thing instead. Some information is best handled by teaching people to hate the practice rather than by circulating the details.

applications.title: Give the practical instructions last and plainly
applications.text: After thirty verses on records and secret plans the counsel becomes ordinary: learn wisdom in thy youth, cry unto God for all thy support, counsel with the Lord in all thy doings, lie down and rise up unto the Lord. Four instructions, all repeatable daily.

applications.title: Watch for the failure that comes from ease
applications.text: The compass worked by faith and stopped when they were slothful, "because those miracles were worked by small means it did show unto them marvelous works. They were slothful." Something that requires almost nothing of you is the easiest thing to stop doing.

applications.title: Do not skip it because it is easy
applications.text: The comparison is made explicit, "it is as easy to give heed to the word of Christ... as it was for our fathers to give heed to this compass." The fathers had a working instrument and perished for not looking at it. Ask what you have that you are not looking at.

questions.text: What am I keeping for a purpose I could not explain if asked?
What small thing have I dismissed as too small to matter?
Where do I keep talking past the edge of what I know?
What do I most need to remember, and how would I make myself?
What do I know that should not be repeated?
What stopped working in my life because I stopped attending to it?
What is easy, available, and untouched?
